theory.what: Assumes no implicit trust — every access request is verified regardless of location.
theory.why: Traditional perimeter fails when attackers get inside. Zero Trust limits lateral movement.
theory.how: Principles: Verify explicitly, Least privilege, Assume breach. Components: Identity, device health, microsegmentation.
theory.when: Implement when modernizing security or after a breach.
theory.configuration:
# Zero Trust steps
1. Identify protect surfaces
2. Map transaction flows
3. Build architecture
4. Create policies
5. Monitor

theory.what: Protects web apps by filtering HTTP traffic — blocks SQLi, XSS, CSRF.
theory.why: Network firewalls cant inspect HTTP payload. WAF understands application protocols.
theory.how: Modes: Detection (log only), Prevention (block). Rules: Signature, Anomaly, Custom. Deploy as reverse proxy or cloud.
theory.when: Deploy in front of all public web applications.
theory.configuration:
# ModSecurity rule
SecRuleEngine On
SecRule ARGS "@detectSQLi" "id:1,deny,status:403"

theory.what: Detecting and filtering attack traffic while allowing legitimate users through.
theory.why: DDoS attacks can take down entire networks.
theory.how: Types: Volumetric (flood), Protocol (SYN flood), Application (HTTP flood). Mitigation: upstream filtering, rate limiting, scrubbing.
theory.when: Implement DDoS protection for all internet-facing services.
theory.configuration:
# Rate limiting
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 80 -m limit --limit 100/s -j ACCEPT

theory.what: Capturing and analyzing packets to troubleshoot and detect attacks.
theory.why: Packet captures show exactly whats happening on the wire.
theory.how: Workflow: Capture → Filter → Analyze → Export. Filters: ip.addr, tcp.port, http.request.
theory.when: Use when troubleshooting connectivity or investigating security incidents.
theory.configuration:
# tcpdump capture
tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap host 10.0.0.1 and port 443

theory.what: Securing DNS against poisoning, tunneling, and using DNS for security filtering.
theory.why: DNS is critical — if it fails everything fails. Also abused for exfiltration and C2.
theory.how: Threats: Cache poisoning, DNS tunneling, DDoS amplification. Protections: DNSSEC, filtering, monitoring.
theory.when: Implement DNS security for all networks. Monitor for anomalies.
theory.configuration:
# DNS filtering
Block: malware.example.com
Block: c2.evil.com
Alert: high query volume to single domain

theory.what: Proper TLS configuration prevents eavesdropping and impersonation.
theory.why: Weak TLS exposes data to interception.
theory.how: Best practices: TLS 1.2+ only, strong ciphers (AES-GCM), HSTS, certificate management.
theory.when: Configure TLS on all services. Disable weak protocols.

theory.what: Collecting and analyzing network evidence for incident investigation.
theory.why: Answers: what happened, when, how, and what was affected.
theory.how: Sources: PCAP, NetFlow, firewall logs, DNS logs, proxy logs. Process: Collect → Analyze → Document → Report.
theory.when: Perform during/after security incidents. Preserve evidence integrity.

theory.what: Ensures only authorized, compliant devices can access the network.
theory.why: Prevents rogue devices and unpatched systems from network access.
theory.how: Components: 802.1X + RADIUS + posture assessment. Non-compliant → quarantine VLAN.
theory.when: Implement on all access ports. Start monitor mode then enforce.
theory.configuration:
# NAC flow
1. Device connects
2. 802.1X auth
3. Posture check
4. Compliant → production
5. Non-compliant → remediation

theory.what: Correlates logs from multiple sources to detect threats.
theory.why: Individual logs show fragments. SIEM correlates to detect advanced threats.
theory.how: Capabilities: Collection, normalization, correlation, alerting, investigation, reporting.
theory.when: Feed: firewalls, IDS, DNS, DHCP, AD, VPN, proxy logs.
theory.configuration:
# Splunk search
index=firewall action=denied | stats count by src_ip | where count > 100

theory.what: Security policies at workload level — controlling east-west traffic.
theory.why: Traditional segmentation is too coarse. Microsegmentation stops lateral movement.
theory.how: Approaches: Host-based firewalls, hypervisor-based (NSX), agent-based (Illumio), cloud-native (SGs).
theory.when: Implement for critical applications and compliance requirements.
theory.configuration:
# Policy example
Web → App: TCP 8080 only
App → DB: TCP 3306 only
Deny all other east-west
